Now there's a problem. The light from the sun has been traveling for some time before it reaches Earth, and during that time, Earth has moved in its orbit around the Sun. As we saw earlier, that movement changes the angle at which the sunlight hits us, so we get different seasons on Earth as the Sun moves along its orbit throughout the year.

## Sizing Up the Sun

The Sun is a star with an enormous radius and mass. Here's what I know about it:

1. The Sun has a diameter of about 70 times that of Earth (about $4 \times 360 = 2,850$ kilometers).
2. It takes 1 year for the Sun to complete one orbit around the center of its star system.
3. The Sun produces energy at an enormous rate. In a lifetime it will produce about as much energy as has been released by all human civilization on Earth since 6,000 B.C.E.

The sun's radius is so big that if you imagine a sphere with this radius and center the earth, then your view of the Sun from Earth is more like looking at an entire ocean. The Sun is not really "in" our solar system; it's just next to us. In fact, from the distance between the earth and sun, most of what we see as a star would look very much like the moon appears on a dark night sky.
